PRESERVATION OF WILDLIFE 
AND ITS HABITAT: 



just one aspect of Stewardship 


National Survival Institute 


"We don't inherit the earth from our grandparent's; we borrow it from our children." 


That quote applies not just to land and minerals but to everything that lives on 
the earth, whether plant or animal, bird or insect. 


There has been human life on this planet for millions of years — human life that 
has shared the earth and not tried to dominate it. It is only in the 20th Century 
that science and technology have offered the temptations of power — and we have 
snatched them without thought or hestitation. But our needs and desires are no 
more important than those of any other living creature, and we have no right to 
impose the effects of our way of life on others. 

However, we are destroying wildlife, and this deprives native people of their tra¬ 
ditional way of life and will leave an impoverished world for our children. 

Do you want your grandchildren 
to hear the cry of a loon on a 
northern lake? 

Can you imagine what it would 
be like if you had never tasted 
fish? 


Why do we need wildlife? 

Human beings are not independent. The world consists of a series of eco-systems — 
patterns of climate, habitat, animal and vegetable life that malfunction if one of 
their component parts is destroyed or weakened. Their inter-relationships are so 
numerous that even now they are not fully understood. Human beings are part of an 
ecosystem, and human life can be affected by damage done to any part of the natural 
environment. 


Wildlife — provides food and drugs. 

Waterfowl and fish are widely used for food, and even the domestic cow was wild once. 
More than 40% of the prescriptions issued in the USA each year contains drug of na¬ 
tural origin — plants, microbes or animals. There are many thousands of species 
whose potential food or medicinal value has not yet been investigated. However, it 
is estimated that between half a million and a million species will have been made 
extinct by the end of the century. This reduction in genetic variety reduces the 
chances of survival of the human race. 

— is important for research. 

Armadillos are invaluable for medical research because they are the only animal 
other than human beings known to contact leprosy. The recent discovery that polar 
bear hairs are exceptionally efficient heat absorbers may lead to better cold wea¬ 
ther clothing and solar energy collectors. The whale's high intelligence could 
throw light on the workings of the human brain. 

— provides ready-made environmental controls. 


Rattlesnakes eat rodents; the nearly extinct peregrine falcon used to control pigeon 
populations in city centres; wolves eat weak animals and so help ensure there is e- 
nough food for the rest of the herd. Shrews are now being imported into Newfoundland 
to help control spruce sawfly. 


(cont. on page 4 


>1 



PRESERVATION OF WILDLIFE (cont. from page 3) 

AND ITS HABITAT: ... 

— acts as a barometer for the state of the 

environment. 

When the effects of pollution start to show in predatory birds or animals — the top 
of the food chain — human beings know that they too are in danger. 

— provides relaxation and enjoyment. 

There are tens of thousands of bird and animal watchers, nature photographers and 
hunters across the country. Canadians spend an estimated $190 million each year 
on wildfowl related activities alone. 

— is an educational tool. 

Many young children relate to wildlife, which can be used to teach them about the 
environment and even lead them to explore social relationships and communication 
among human beings. 

What are the threats to wildlife? 

Destruction of habitat. 

Suburbs, roads, airports and shopping malls are built over nesting and feeding areas; 
marsh land is "reclaimed" because it is felt to be unproductive: forests are clear- 
stripped; fish breeding grounds are silted up with eroded soil and the debris from 
construction projects. 

One of the last areas where wild-life habitat is relatively undisturbed is the Artie. 
But now oil and mineral wealth are threatening even this "last frontier." The Demp¬ 
ster Highway, which opened in 1978, bisects the range of the Porcupine caribou herd, 
one of the last great herds in the world. It is not yet known what effect this re¬ 
striction on movement will have on the herd, but hunters have been shooting the ani¬ 
mals from their cars. Gravel for roads is dug from the denning areas of fox, wolves 
and bears. Low-flying aircraft frighten herds of caribou; animals break their legs 
in the stampede and mothers are separated from their young. Polar bears investigate 

construction camps and are shot. Finally - the greatest danger - no one knows 

whether an oil spill in Artie waters could be contained. The Arctic food chains are 
simple, relying heavily on a group of shrimp-like creatures. An oil spill which kil¬ 
led these creatures would have devastating effects on all Artie animals and thus on 
the native people who rely on them for food. 

Over-exploitation by hunting and fishing. 

The George River caribou herd, said to be the largest free-ranging herd in the world, 
may be endangered because of excessive hunting in Northern Quebec. 

Overfishing has two consequences — direct reduction of the species being fished, 
and accidental removal of smaller species that form the basis of the marine food 
chain. This "incidental take" is estimated to destroy 7 million tonnes of fish each 
year. 

Introduction of alien species. 

The Garrison Diversion project designed to irrigate land in North Dakota, will trans¬ 
fer fish, diseases and parasites native to the Missouri River watershed to the Hudson 
Bay system, threatening the existence of commercial fisheries in Lake Winnipeg and 
Lake Manitoba. 

Poisoning 

Pesticides and herbicides harm birds and animals. The peregrine falcon, the fastest 
creature in the world, with a diving speed of 250 kilometers an hour, was brought to 
the brink of extinction by pesticides.

THE C.C.A. 


L'A.C.C. 


The C.C.A. was founded in 1936 as anon- 
profit organization. It is a national 
federation of provincial camping asso¬ 
ciations uniting the camping leaders 
into an organization involved in the 
growth, development and promotion of 
camping in Canada. 

All Canadian Camping Association pro¬ 
grams and projects are made possible by 
membership fees, private contributions 
and funds from Fitness and Amateur 
Sport, Government of Canada. 

The Canadian Camping Association oper¬ 
ates a bookstore, primarily as a ser¬ 
vice to its members. Books of interest 
to camp directors, administrators, par¬ 
ents, counsellors and leaders working 
with children and youth in the outdoors 
are available in the Toronto office or 
may be ordered by mail or telephone. 

The books handled by C.C.A. are classi¬ 
fied into broad categories and listed 
alphabetically along with a brief de¬ 
scription of their contents, the pub¬ 
lisher and the price. There is an al¬ 
phabetical index and order forms at the 
end of this catalogue. 


L ! Association des camps du Canada, creee 
en 1936, est un organisme a but non lucratif 
et une federation nationale des associations 
provinciales de camping reunissant les orga- 
nismes qui se vouent a la croissance et a 
l f expansion du camping au Canada. 

Tous les projets et programmes de 1'Association 
canadienne des camps sont realises grace aux 
cotisations des membres, aux contributions des 
particuliers et aux subventions de la Direction 
generale de la Condition physique et du Sport 
amateur du gouvernement federal. 

L f Association canadienne des camps offre un 
service de librairie a ses membres. Les livres 
interessant les responsables de camps d'enfants 
et d'adolescents (directeurs, administrateurs, 
parents, conseillers et moniteurs) sont dispo- 
nibles au siege social a Toronto. On accepte 
les commandes telephoniques ou postales. 

Nos publications sont divisees en categories 
generales. La liste alphabetique contient un 
resume succinct de chaque publication et indi- 
que l'editeur et le prix. A la fin du catalo¬ 
gue se trouvent la liste alphabetique des 
livres et des bons de commande. 






As well as selling books from both Ca¬ 
nadian and American sources, the C.C.A. 
publishes a number of titles and is the 
sole distributor in Canada for books 
published by the American Camping Asso¬ 
ciation.

PROJECT REACH 

These materials developed by Project Reach deal especially with the expansion 
and development of camping with the handicapped, although they are applicable 
to every camp in many ways. They are available to the Canadian Camping Asso¬ 
ciation from the American Camping Association. Project Reach is funded by the 
U.S. Department of Health, Education and Welfare and is located at the Univer¬ 
sity of Kentucky at Lexington. Four categories are planned.

PRESERVATION OF WILDLIFE 
AND ITS HABITAT: 


(cont. from page 4) 


Acid rain is killing fish in the lakes and rivers of Eastern Canada. In Ontario 
alone some 200 lakes are already "dead" and 48,000 may be lost by the turn of the 
century. 

Between 1962 and 1970 Dryden Chemicals Ltd. dumped nearly 10,000 kilograms (20,000 lbs) 
of mercury into the English-Wabigoon River system in North-western Ontario, making its 
fish — the staple diet of the Indian villages of White Dog and Grassy Narrows — un¬ 
safe to eat. 

In 1979 the Federal Government made a special regulation allowing Amax of Canada to 
dump molybdenum mine tailings into Alice Arm, an inlet of the Pacific in Northern 
British Columbia. One hundred million metric tons will be dumped over a 26 year 
period. The tailings will be concentrations 16,000 times higher than allowed by the 
Fisheries Act, and will contain arsenic, lead, mercury, cadmium, copper, zinc, iron 
and Radium 226. Scientific reports and eveidence from twother sites where tailings 
have been dumped into the sea — in lower concentrations — indicate very strongly 
that marine life will be affected and will pose a danger to human life. Alice Arm 
is the traditional fishing ground of the Nishga Indians, and provides their main source 
of food. 

What hope is there? 

An example to follow: 

Seven major Canadian churches have opposed the Alice Arm dumping, together with nu¬ 
merous organizations including the B.C. Medical Organization, the B.C. Federation of 
Labour and miners belonging to the United Steelworkers of America. The Anglican 
Church bought Amax shares and put forward a resolution at the 1981 shareholders' 
meeting asking for a moratorium on the dumping until a public hearing was held. 

Other gleams of hope for wildlife: 

* The Mackenzie Valley Pipeline Inquiry, headed by Justice Thomas Berger, proposed 
the establishment of bird and whale sanctuaries in the Mackenzie Delta and a Na¬ 
tional Wilderness Park to protect the wildlife of the Nothern Yukon. 

!- * Peregrine falcons and whooping cranes, once nearly extinct, now seem more likely 
to survive. Peregrine falcons are being bred at centres in Alberta, Saskatchewan 
and Quebec and released in the wild. Whooping crane eggs from Wood Buffalo Na¬ 
tional Park in the Northwest Territories are being hatched by sandhill cranes on 
a reserve in Idaho. 

* An organization called Ducks Unlimited has undertaken more than 1600 projects across 
Canada, creating almost 2.6 million acres of good waterfowl habitat. 

i What can I do to help? 

Walk along a nature trail or go to a Natural Science museum and learn how an eco¬ 
system works. 

Join a wildlife association — 

Write to your elected representative about the need to preserve wildlife. 

Support the preservation of wildlife habitat in your area. 

Write to the presidents of companies that dump toxic wates in oceans or rivers. - “ 

Boycott their products. . . 

(cont. on page24 ) 




RAPPORT SPECIAL 


SPECIAL REPORT 


par Rosaire Corbin, 
directeur g€ndral - 
A ■ C • Q • 


’'ON A BESOIN DE VOUS; C'EST POUR VOUS!'' 


Pour une Association ei. qui on confie le mandat de representer ses mem- 
bres, de promouvoir et d6£endre leurs interets, il est impensable qu' 
elle remplisse adequatement ce role si elle ne dispose pas des donnSes 
de base qui caract6risent 1'ensemble de son membership. 

Dans le jargon modeme, on appelle cela des statistiques. Meme si on 
rSp&te que "les chiffres ne veulent rien dire ou encore qu'on peut faire 
dire ce qu'on veut aux statistiques", il n'en reste pas moins que le lan¬ 
guage des chiffres est tres Eloquent. 

Qui que nous soyons, nous sommes toujours a la recherche des chiffres, la 
saine gestion d'uncamp ou d'une Association en depend. 

Les membres du Conseild'administration ou des Comit6s ont sans cesse be- 
soin d'un portrait fidele de ses membres pour mieux assumer leurs fonctions. 
La quality et 1'impact de leurs interventions sont etroitement li§s h la 
connaissance qu'ils ont du milieu qu'ils reprgsentent. 

Quoi de plus difficile d'entamer une discussion ou une negociation lors- 
qu'aux premieres questions posees: "qui reprSsentez-vous?, combien d'en- 
fants accueillez-vous dans vos camps? combien de personnes engagez-vous? 
il faut faire precSder les r6ponses des mots "Il peu pres" la solidite de 
1*argumentation en est automatiquement affaiblie. 

On ne saurait trop insister sur la necessity de r6pondre aux differents 
questionnaires qui vous sont envoyes par votre Association. N6gliger 
de le faire aux dates prevues paralysent 1'action de vos repr6sentants 
et est prejudiciable aux autres membres. 

Si on est fier de notre entreprise, si on est fier de notre action aupres 
des personnes qui frequentent nos camps, on se doit de ripandre ces bonnes 
nouvelles. Le public doit le savoir, les institutions gouvemementales 
ou autres doivent le savoir-, car nous contribuons par nos activites au 
developpement des personnes, au developpement social et au dSveloppement 
economique. Cela nous le savons, mais pour le faire connaitre globale- 
ment aux autres, il faut des donnies, il faut des statistiques. 


22 





Innombrables sont ceux qui s'adressent aux Associations pour connaitre 
ou mieux connaitre le domaine des camps. Tantot ce sont des institu¬ 
tions de recherche, tels les universitds et les colleges, tantot ce 
sont les institutions gouvemementales-, tantot ce sont les federations 
de sport ou de loisir, tantot ce sont d'eventuels membres commerciaux. 

Vos representants ou vos employes se trouvent souvent dans des situa¬ 
tions embetantes car ils ne peuvent avec fermete et certitude etablir 
clairement le portrait exact des camps. 

Comme suite aux renseignements recueillis l'an dernier voici quelques 
donnees statistiques. Elies ont la valeur objective de savants cal- 
culs d'extrapolation effectues afin de remedier aux 451 des non-re- 
pondants. 

II est a esperer une reponse de la totality des camps afin de donner 
plus de credibility a nos statistiques. 

II n'en tient qu'& vous; car c'est pour vous!!!

PRESERVATION OF WILDLIFE 
AND ITS HABITAT: 

(cont from page 21 ) 

Borrow a film on wildlife from the 
National Film Board or the World Wild¬ 
life Fund and show it to your friends. 


For children, there are two nature 
magazines, Chickadee (up to age eight) 
and Owl (eight to twelve), available at 
newsstands or by subscription from: 


Young Naturalists’ Foundation 
59 Front Street E. 

Toronto, Ontario KIP 5E7 



Start a children’s Wildlife Club. 

Put a bird feeder in your back yard.
